item.title: Peltola campaign's alleged Dan Sullivan spoiler plot takes new turn as DOJ faces major legal hurdle
item.description: The Department of Justice's Alaska Senate race lawsuit faces hurdles as legal scholars debate whether anonymous ballot analysis can prove confusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Justice faces an uphill legal battle in Alaska, where it is trying to convince a federal court that confusion between two Senate candidates with nearly identical names could be enough to delay certification of the election results.

Roughly two weeks before Election Day on Oct. 22, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking to delay certification if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses and votes cast for another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could have changed the result, pending an investigation into whether voters mistakenly selected the wrong candidate.

The DOJ's complaint stems from a controversy in Alaska where two individuals by the name of Dan Sullivan, one a retired school teacher and the other the state’s incumbent senator, appear alongside each other on the state’s ballots. Although Alaska has traditionally been a Republican stronghold in Senate elections, the state's race could carry greater national significance this year as Republicans seek to defend their narrow Senate majority.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that the campaign of Mary Peltola, the Democrat running for Senate in Alaska, reportedly worked with operatives to recruit another Dan Sullivan to run for Alaska’s Senate seat, hoping voter confusion would draw support from the incumbent Republican senator. Citing interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit, the Times reported that the effort also targeted other potential spoiler candidates, despite the Peltola campaign’s repeated denials of involvement in the second Sullivan’s candidacy.

TODD BLANCHE CHALLENGES DANA BASH FOR ONLY CITING PART OF CONSTITUTION DURING HEATED ELECTION CLASH

On Sunday, Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee filed a proposed motion to dismiss the Justice Department's lawsuit, arguing that the federal law cited by the DOJ governs voter registration, not candidate eligibility or ballot design. They also urged the court to resolve the case before Election Day.

Conservatives have argued that two similar names on the same ballot could possibly lead to voters who would prefer to reelect the state’s Republican senator accidentally voting for the retired school teacher. Opponents of the effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot argue that sharing a name with an incumbent is not grounds for disqualification and that Alaska's ranked-choice voting system allows voters to rank both candidates, potentially limiting the effects of mistaken selections.

Alaska’s Division of Elections initially sided with conservatives, disqualifying Sullivan the school teacher by finding that his candidacy was not a genuine, good-faith bid for office but instead was designed to confuse voters into mistaking him for the senator. Alaska Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews overturned the decision in June, holding that the Division of Elections had no authority to void a candidacy on that basis.

Alaska's general election ballot identifies the incumbent as "Sullivan, Dan S.," with Republican and incumbent designations, while listing the other candidate as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," without a party affiliation, a measure some argue is enough to clear up potential confusion. Lawyers at the Justice Department, however, remain unconvinced.

Although Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested that officials could examine ranked-choice ballot patterns for signs of confusion, the Justice Department has not explained how those patterns could establish that individual voters mistakenly selected the wrong candidate. Voter privacy protections pose a major obstacle to a potential federal case, as it would be nigh impossible to tie specific voters to specific ballots to serve as evidence of confusion.

ALASKA HAS A VOTING SYSTEM LIKE NO OTHER STATE; REPUBLICANS WORRY IT COULD COST THEM IN NOVEMBER

"This is just the stuff that is just impossible to measure after the fact," Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller said of the DOJ’s plan to infer voter intentions from anonymous ballots.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in interviews with the press, has provided some insight into how he would like the DOJ to go about solving this problem.

"So because of rank-based voting, voters … they write not just one, not just two, but multiple names on the ballot. And so there are a number of scenarios where it could be obvious that a voter was confused by the way they wrote down candidates," Blanche told CNN’s Dana Bash.

Blanche's comments suggest that the Justice Department could examine ranked-choice ballot patterns for potential signs of confusion, although such patterns alone would not establish whether voters intended to support a different candidate.

"It will be obvious from the results and from the ballots that voters were confused, and that could be obvious from the way that they rank the Dan Sullivans or not including a Dan Sullivan on the ballot," he said in a later interview with CBS.

ALASKA REPUBLICANS SCRAMBLE TO EDUCATE VOTERS ON SUSPECTED DEM PLANT AS 'BALLOT FATIGUE' THREATENS RACE

Don Palmer, senior legal fellow for election integrity at the right-of-center Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital that he feels the Justice Department might have a case if the agency's lawyers construct it properly. Statistical analysis of ballots alone, he maintains, will likely not be sufficient to convince a judge of the administration's position. 

"You'll have the opportunity to interview witnesses, do some statistical analysis, and make a decision whether or not the campaign wants to contest the results of the election," Palmer said. "So it's actually quite a high standard where you have to bring in witnesses. You can't generally just prove it with some statistical analysis … the campaign would have to show to the court through statistical and expert testimony, plus witness testimony, plus affidavits, that enough voters were confused, that they made inaccurate choices on what they intended to do. Then and only then could the court determine whether the race should be overturned."

"If voters voted for the non-Republican Dan Sullivan as their 1st choice but voted down ballot for Republicans as their 1st choice otherwise, that could indicate patterns of confusion whereby voters were looking to vote straight Republican as their first choice and were prevented from doing so because the inclusion of Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot confused matters," a spokesman for the America First Policy Institute told Fox News Digital.

Ben Hovland, a senior fellow at the left-of-center Center for American Progress and an expert on elections, was more bearish on the DOJ’s prospects.

SEEING DOUBLE: SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES, SETTING UP BIZARRE ALASKA SENATE BALLOT

"You've never seen a claim like this made under the National Voter Registration Act," he told Fox News Digital. "This is not a matter of federal law. This is a state ballot qualification issue and the Alaska Supreme Court addressed this issue months ago. For the Department of Justice to step in at this point and sort of make this claim, you know, doesn't appear to be about winning in a lawsuit because it doesn't seem like there's any scenario where [they win], this is clearly about trying to sow confusion or sow doubt or set the stage to undermine the results of the election if the administration doesn't like what the voters will have to say."

Walter Olson, a senior legal fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute, also isn't convinced that the Justice Department will be able to get its case off the ground.

"I wouldn't expect Blanche's local allies to get very far in this effort unless a federal court rules in favor of his theory that Alaska violated federal (as opposed to state) law by letting the schoolteacher stay on the ballot," Olson told Fox News Digital. "I think the state is likely to beat Blanche in federal court on that point, and that should end the case."

Alaska has already moved to have the DOJ's case dismissed.

The DOJ did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

item.title: FBI reports 67% jump in violent crime arrests under Trump compared to Biden’s final months
item.description: Kash Patel says the FBI arrested over 47,000 violent criminals and gang members in 21 months, marking a 67% increase over the Biden era.
item.content:encoded:
The FBI has made significant gains in combating crime and arresting violent offenders and child predators over the past 21 months under the Trump administration, according to data released by the agency on Wednesday.

In that timeframe, the FBI arrested more than 47, 000 violent criminals and gang members — a 67% increase compared to the final 21 months of the Biden administration.

Arrests of child sex predators and human traffickers also rose 13%, reaching just over 6,000, agency figures show.

KASH PATEL TO TOUT 'LARGEST' YEAR-TO-YEAR VIOLENT CRIME DROP IN US HISTORY

"Over the last 21 months under the Trump administration’s leadership and working alongside our Department of Justice and law enforcement partners, this FBI has delivered the largest reduction in violent crime in United States history," said FBI Director Kash Patel.

Patel highlighted several key metrics, including a 30% drop in the national murder rate, a 114% increase in violent crime suspect arrests, and the seizure of over 4,600 kilograms of fentanyl — an amount capable of killing more than 350 million Americans.

FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18%

Additionally, law enforcement apprehended 10 of the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted fugitives, 2.5 times the number captured over the previous four years, as well as six fugitives from a newly created "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list within its first four months.

The FBI faced intense criticism from Republicans during the Biden administration over allegations of political bias, government overreach, and its handling of high-profile investigations.

KASH PATEL DEFENDS FBI'S ‘MOST WANTED’ BUSTS AMID MANIPULATION ACCUSATIONS, HIGHLIGHTS 'SUMMER HEAT' SUCCESS

Addressing the shift, Patel added that his agency faced one of the highest threat environments in American history when Trump began his second term.

"This FBI and law enforcement responded by delivering in the biggest way they ever have," he said. "This is what happens with a President who backs the blue, an Attorney General who relentlessly prosecutes criminals, and good cops all over the country getting the job done."

item.title: 50,000 airline miles stolen from a travel expert
item.description: Travel expert Katy Nastro says 50,000 American Airlines AAdvantage miles vanished from her account after someone redeemed them without permission.
item.content:encoded:
If you're anything like me, you've probably spent years collecting airline miles, dreaming about the trip you'll eventually take. Maybe it's a business class seat to Europe or that vacation you've been putting off. You keep earning points and watching the balance grow. But what happens when you finally check your account and discover someone else has already spent them?

That's exactly what happened to Katy Nastro, a travel expert with Flighty, a flight-tracking app that provides real-time updates on delays, cancellations and gate changes. During our conversation on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast, Katy shared how more than 50,000 American Airlines miles vanished from her account. Someone had redeemed them for a flight without her permission.

What surprised me was that Katy knows the travel industry inside and out. Yet she still found herself dealing with a problem that could happen to anyone with a frequent flyer account. Her experience offers a warning, especially as holiday travel approaches.

9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET/8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Katy had just landed in New York and was riding home in an Uber. Like many frequent travelers, she opened her American Airlines app to check how many miles she'd earned from her latest trip. Instead, she noticed a substantial drop in her balance. At first, she figured the app had made a mistake. She remembered redeeming about 10,000 miles recently, but the balance was off by roughly 50,000. So she refreshed the app. The missing miles were still missing. That's when she called American Airlines.

The airline told her that someone had redeemed the miles for a ticket in another person's name. Katy had been saving for a trip to Asia. Unfortunately, those miles were now associated with a flight she knew nothing about. 

"I really had this just stomach drop moment," Katy told me.

She had spent years earning those rewards, including through long flights to Australia. Suddenly, someone else had benefited from all that travel. 

"I naively never thought this could happen to me because I work in the industry," she admitted. 

I found that particularly revealing. Katy had previously warned people about loyalty account theft. Even with that experience, she never expected to become a victim herself.

You might assume the airline could simply reverse an unauthorized redemption. After all, the ticket was booked in someone else's name. Unfortunately, Katy discovered that getting her miles back required additional work. American Airlines instructed her to submit a formal fraud complaint by email. She also had to file a police report and provide documentation before the airline would restore her miles. 

"I had to have the police report filed with them before anything was credited," Katy explained.

She eventually recovered her miles, but the process didn't end there. Katy also had to create a new email address and establish a replacement American Airlines AAdvantage account. Thankfully, the airline transferred her existing status along with her restored rewards. What caught my attention was the police report requirement. Katy had to involve local law enforcement even though the theft happened entirely online. She understood why the airline might want official documentation, but she questioned whether the process needed to be so cumbersome.

There's another concern for travelers. Airline loyalty points generally don't carry the same protections as money stolen through an unauthorized credit card purchase. In fact, American Airlines' current AAdvantage terms say the airline has no general obligation to restore miles withdrawn without authorization. 

The company may review requests submitted within three months of the unauthorized withdrawal, but reimbursement remains discretionary. That makes discovering suspicious activity quickly especially important. Also, keep in mind that each loyalty program has its own fraud procedures. A police report may be requested, but the requirement isn't universal.

I asked Katy something that had been bothering me. Who was actually flying around using her miles? She had no idea. The airline identified a redemption involving someone else's name, but Katy didn't know who was behind it or where the traveler was headed. Loyalty programs often allow members to book tickets for other people. Some also permit mileage transfers or gifts. Those legitimate features can create opportunities for criminals who gain unauthorized access to an account.

For example, someone who controls your account could redeem miles for a ticket under another person's name. Depending on the program, the points might also be transferred or exchanged for other rewards. However, Katy never learned exactly how someone accessed her account. During our conversation, she acknowledged that password reuse may have played a role. 

"I think I fell into the trap of using the same password for everything," she said.

That's an easy habit to fall into. If criminals obtain a password from one compromised service, they may try using it to access other accounts. And here's something worth remembering. A loyalty balance may look like a collection of numbers on your screen, but those numbers can pay for expensive flights.

Katy shared another piece of advice that might surprise anyone who's been patiently saving miles for years. She believes travelers should think twice about holding on to their rewards indefinitely. 

"I would highly suggest that you should not be waiting on those miles," she told me. 

Her concern comes down to depreciation. Airlines can change their award pricing, which means a flight that once required 50,000 miles might eventually require considerably more. I compared holding on to miles to buying a new car and watching its value drop after driving off the lot. Katy agreed. In her view, people often wait too long for that perfect first-class redemption. She recommends considering redemptions within a year instead of endlessly saving for a future trip.

Of course, you still want to check whether an award flight offers reasonable value. Spending 80,000 miles on an inexpensive economy ticket could be a poor deal. However, if you need to travel during a busy holiday period, using miles for an economy seat may make sense. 

Award tickets can also offer more flexibility than certain restrictive cash fares. Just check the airline's cancellation and redeposit rules before booking. We've shared more strategies in our article, Are airline miles still worth it? 

And if you're looking to earn more rewards for your next trip, check out my picks for the best airline credit cards of 2026 at CyberGuy.com to see which programs might work best for you.

YOUR CREDIT CAN LOOK NORMAL WHILE SOMEONE STEALS YOUR IDENTITY

Watch out for fake airline alerts and customer service scams

During our conversation, I told Katy about something I've been seeing more frequently. I receive emails that look like legitimate airline notifications, claiming miles were redeemed from my account. Some are convincing enough that I've nearly clicked them myself. That's a particularly sneaky approach because many airlines send real notifications when members redeem rewards. Criminals can imitate those messages to create panic and lure people toward fake login pages.

Katy warned that scammers also create fake airline support accounts on social media. Someone looking for help with a delayed flight or missing miles might contact what appears to be an official account. The conversation can then move to a private message or even WhatsApp, where the criminal asks for personal information. Katy's warning was clear. Avoid sharing sensitive account information through social media conversations. If you receive a suspicious redemption notice, open the airline's official app yourself. Check your account activity directly rather than following links in the message.

Before your next trip, take a few minutes to secure the loyalty accounts you've spent years building. These steps can help you spot unauthorized activity sooner and make your accounts harder to compromise.

Open your airline and hotel loyalty apps at least once a month. Review recent redemptions and compare your current balance with what you expected. Katy said she sometimes went several months without checking her account. That made it harder to know when the unauthorized redemption occurred. Setting a recurring calendar reminder can help you catch unusual activity sooner. Also, enable account activity and redemption alerts if your loyalty program offers them. That way, you may find out about suspicious transactions before you notice missing miles.

Never reuse your airline password on another website. A password manager can generate strong, unique passwords and store them securely. Also, protect the email account connected to your loyalty program. Someone who gains access to that inbox may be able to reset your rewards password.

Look for two-factor authentication (2FA), passkeys or other login verification options offered by your airline or hotel program. These protections vary by provider, so check your account's security settings. Also, review any unfamiliar changes to your contact information and remove devices or sessions you no longer recognize when the service allows it.

If an email or text claims someone used your points, resist clicking its links. Instead, open the official airline app or type the website address into your browser. Legitimate-looking logos and familiar formatting offer no guarantee that a message is genuine. 

Also, be skeptical of anyone claiming to represent airline support through an unsolicited social media message. Use strong antivirus software to help detect malicious links, block dangerous websites and protect against malware designed to steal your passwords. While antivirus software can't stop every phishing scam, it provides an additional layer of protection if you accidentally click something suspicious.

FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS

Contact your loyalty program through its verified customer service channels as soon as you notice an unauthorized redemption. Ask the airline to secure your account and investigate the transaction. Save your account statements and any correspondence. If the airline requests a police report, follow its instructions and keep a copy. Don't delay because some programs impose deadlines on fraud claims.

Katy suggested using a dedicated email address for loyalty programs. That can make account notifications easier to track and reduce exposure if an unrelated service suffers a breach. Another option is to use an email alias, which helps keep your primary address private. It lets you create unlimited email aliases, helping you organize travel accounts while reducing spam and unwanted exposure. You can also follow my guide on how to create and use email aliases. 

For recommendations on private and secure email providers that offer alias addresses, visit CyberGuy.com.

Your personal information may already be circulating on data broker websites, making it easier for scammers to target you with convincing airline phishing emails or impersonation attempts. Consider using a personal data removal service. It helps remove your personal information from hundreds of data broker and people search sites and continues submitting removal requests when your details reappear. While no service can erase everything or directly prevent someone from stealing your airline miles, reducing your online exposure can make it harder for scammers to gather personal details and tailor their attacks. 

Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Be careful about sharing photos of boarding passes, luggage tags or travel confirmations online. These documents can contain booking reference numbers, frequent flyer details or barcodes that expose information about your trip. Criminals may use those details to access reservations or impersonate travelers. Avoid posting travel documents on social media, and securely dispose of printed boarding passes after your trip.

You can use an AI assistant like ChatGPT with scheduled tasks to monitor airline loyalty programs for changes that could reduce the value of your miles. Set up a daily alert to check for announced changes to redemption rates, award pricing or loyalty program rules. You can even ask it to track news about American Airlines AAdvantage or other programs you use. 

That way, you may hear about upcoming changes while there's still time to redeem your miles at current rates. Keep in mind that airlines don't always announce devaluations in advance, so AI can't predict every change. For step-by-step guidance, check out my article on 8 seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent.

I keep thinking about Katy sitting in the back of that Uber, casually checking her mileage balance and discovering that 50,000 hard-earned miles had disappeared. I've collected airline miles for years, and I know how much planning goes into using them. The thought of some stranger enjoying a trip on my points would make me furious. What concerns me even more is that Katy works in the travel industry and still couldn't explain exactly how someone got into her account. 

That tells me we should give our loyalty accounts the same attention we give our financial accounts. Check your balances, use unique passwords and pay attention to unusual activity. And while I love saving miles for a great trip, Katy makes a convincing argument for enjoying those rewards while they still offer good value.

I encourage you to listen to The CyberGuy Report podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/ to hear my full conversation with Katy Nastro. item.title: Maryland is going to some embarrassing lengths to make sure students stay until the end of games
item.description: The Maryland Terrapins are raffling free spring tuition to keep students in the stadium through their Halloween college football game against Illinois.
item.content:encoded:
For some college football programs, getting students to stay in their seats until the final whistle is no problem. In fact, in some cases it might even be harder to get them to leave.

However, for other schools, especially those struggling on the field, the students may need some convincing to hang around until the game goes final.

Unfortunately, the Maryland Terrapins fall into the latter camp, and they're going to some wild lengths to keep students from going home and studying... or more likely, getting blasted in the parking lot.

The Terps are 2-5 on the year, 0-4 in Big Ten play, and just fired head coach Mike Locksley. That's usually a recipe for making it hard to keep students in the stadium.

No one wants to stand there and watch their team lose when the Tri-Delts are dishing out free Jell-O shots down the street.

So, with the Illinois Illini coming to town on Halloween, they decided to raffle off free spring tuition to one lucky student... who stays in the stadium through the end of the game.

ARIZONA FOOTBALL COACH PURCHASES $2,000 WORTH OF TEQUILA FOR FANS IN FIVE-MINUTES AFTER IOWA STATE WIN

That's awesome for whoever wins, but man, as a program, this is not good.

For some reason, it wouldn't seem as bad if they were raffling some Amazon gift cards or free Papa John's pizza (which is as much as you should ever pay for one of those).

Offering the chance to win free tuition — thousands of dollars — to sit through a college football game is rough.

Still, I am sure this will work wonders. Ask anyone who's paying off their student loans. Forget staying until the game ends; I'd chain myself to the stadium for a free semester (still open to this, by the way).

The downside is that this little tidbit of info is now out on social media, which means any team that plays Maryland just got serious ammunition for opposing fans to use against them.

item.title: Democrat House candidate hit with felony summons at campaign event
item.description: Lakesha Womack, who is running for the U.S. House of Representatives, said she was served with felony rental car charges at her own North Carolina campaign event.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic candidate running for the U.S. House of Representatives said she is facing criminal charges and that she was hit with a police summons while at her own campaign event this month.

Lakesha Womack, who is running to represent North Carolina's 14th Congressional District, which is currently held by Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., said in a Facebook video she was confronted by police about felony charges related to failure to pay for a rental car in 2019 when she arrived to a campaign event in Polk County, N.C., on Oct. 11. 

Womack claimed she was first made aware of the felony case just days before despite records showing it had been opened in January 2020.

Moore's campaign said the incident "raises serious questions" and that "she owes voters an explanation, especially since her court date is one week after the election."

DEM HOUSE CANDIDATE SETTLES YEARS-LONG $55K DEBT FIGHT WITH FORMER MOTHER-IN-LAW WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION

"How is she going to be an advocate for our community when she can't manage her own personal affairs? As an attorney for over 30 years, I think everyone should be held to the same standard of justice, and this situation is no different. Free legal advice: When the rental agreement ends, so does your right to keep the car," Moore's campaign told Fox News Digital.

The Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office confirmed to Fox News Digital that Womack was served a criminal summons for felony failure to return a hired motor vehicle on Oct. 11 by a deputy with the Polk County Sheriff’s Office. It did not confirm that it took place at a campaign event.

DEMOCRAT CANDIDATE SEEN SOBBING, PRAYING IN PATROL CAR AFTER DUI ARREST: VIDEO

Womack recalled being told about her criminal charges days before the campaign event during a conversation with Gastonia, North Carolina's NAACP branch. In 2019, she said she was homeless with little money when she had a medical incident that sent her to the intensive care unit (ICU). During that time, her son was placed into foster care with no one immediately able to look after him.

After retrieving her son, Womack said, "I'm living in a hotel and, you know, scraping together, you know, dollars to buy food from Dollar Tree, to like, buy dinner for him every night. And I had a rental car. Couldn't afford the rental car, and they came and got it. And, so, I never knew that, you know, they have filed, you know, I guess that it was a pending felony.

DEM HOUSE HOPEFUL ALLEGES SHE WAS BRUTALLY ATTACKED DURING 2 AM CAMPAIGN ERRAND

"I didn't post that I was gonna be in Polk County, but they knew exactly what car I was driving. And as soon as I parked, they pulled up behind me and served my papers with my address from 2019. So, y'all hadn't looked for me in the past seven years, but now all of a sudden, you know exactly what car I drive and where I'm going to be," Womack said.

She did admit in an Oct. 9 video addressing the charges that she did owe fees, "but I just want you all to know that, you know, I do owe them people some money." She said in the same video that she thought she previously "had resolved the issue, but it’s not resolved."

Womack said in that video that she could not receive the January 2020 criminal summons at the time because she was homeless and therefore did not have a stable address.

That video appears to have since been deleted from her campaign Facebook page. Womack said in later videos that she could not discuss an active case.

If found guilty, she could face between four and 24 months behind bars or community service for that duration.

North Carolina's 14th Congressional District is located in the western part of the state and spans from the suburbs of Charlotte to more rural areas in the North Carolina foothills.

Fox News Digital reached out to Womack's campaign for comment.

item.title: Islanders star Matthew Schaefer pulls off an NHL first that sounds absolutely exhausting
item.description: Matthew Schaefer became the first player in at least 15 years to stay on the ice for an entire three-on-three overtime in a wild Islanders game.
item.content:encoded:
The average shift in the National Hockey League is well under one minute before a player hops back over the boards, but tell that to New York Islanders star defenseman Matthew Schaefer.

The Islanders paid a visit to the Nashville Predators on Tuesday night, in what turned into a wild game.

New York built up a 3-0 lead, but the Predators rallied with three unanswered goals to force overtime.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

That is where we saw Schaefer do something that has never been seen since the NHL started tracking this kind of data in 2009-10.

Schaefer, the reigning Calder Trophy winner, is a dynamic two-way defenseman, which means he was practically purpose-built for 3-on-3 overtime. So, unsurprisingly, head coach Peter DeBoer sent the 19-year-old out to get the extra frame started.

Schaefer stayed on the ice for the first half of the extra period before Nashville's Filip Forsberg tripped him, forcing the period's first stoppage.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The top pick in the 2025 NHL Draft quarterbacks the Isles' top power play unit, which is more than likely why DeBoer used a timeout to give his boys a rest.

When play resumed, Schaefer stayed on the ice for the rest of overtime.

That made him the first player in at least fifteen years to stay on the ice for the entirety of a 3-on-3 overtime.

That sounds brutal. Sure, the timeout and the fact that the second half of OT was almost exclusively in the Nashville zone due to the power play helped make it happen, but that is some insane endurance.

While the Isles needed a shootout to win the game 4-3, Schaefer logged a whopping 32:16, which, per Sportsnet, is the third-highest single-game total for any player this season.

Schaefer also had an assist in the game, giving him 11 points (2G, 9A) on the year, putting him at just under a point-per-game pace.

item.title: Hochul reveals which election result would make her job 'a lot easier' — and it's not her own
item.description: Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she privately cautioned Israel against overreach after Oct. 7 and questioned Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Tuesday that her job would be "a lot easier" if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses his bid to remain in power.

"A lot easier. And here’s the challenge: I represent the largest Jewish population in the world outside of Israel," Hochul told Politico Magazine when asked "How much easier would your job get if [Benjamin] Netanyahu loses?"

"And I know they’re suffering," Hochul continued. "A lot of people are anxious about antisemitism, which is sky-high right now. And I take that personally, because I represent everyone. I went to Israel right after Oct. 7. I saw a lot of pain there. But I actually cautioned the government there, in private conversations, not to overreach."

Israelis cast their ballots on Tuesday in the country's first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre. Tuesday's election in Israel notably came just one week before the U.S. midterm elections – which includes Hochul's race to retain her position as New York's top leader.

POTENTIAL 2028 DEM CONTENDER UNLOADS ON NETANYAHU, ADMITS US-ISRAEL TIES AT 'CROSSROADS'

"The world is with you when it comes to the brutal assault by a terrorist organization known as Hamas on innocent Israeli people," she continued. "An overreach could change that dynamic, and that’s what’s happened."

The Democratic governor went on to say that she does not believe it is currently in Netanyahu's "interest" to "have a safe Palestinian state."

Hochul is not the only prominent New York Democrat to criticize Netanyahu. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has been even more outspoken, calling the Israeli leader "the architect of horrific genocide against Palestinians" in September.

Hochul is also facing voters in November, but a Siena Research Institute poll released Wednesday showed her holding a 14-point lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, 54% to 40%.

RAHM EMANUEL ACCUSES ANTI-ISRAEL DEMS OF HAVING NO MIDDLE EAST PLAN BESIDES CUTTING FUNDING TO JEWISH STATE

Hochul notably issued a proclamation on May 11 recognizing the month as Jewish American Heritage Month in her state.

"We have to have leadership there that understands the security of Israel is paramount — critically important to me, but also the world — but to have a safe Palestinian state as well, which has been talked about my entire life," Hochul told Politico Magazine. "I still believe that this can happen. I believe we have to get people of goodwill who can make this happen, and as long as Netanyahu is sitting there, that is not in his interest to do that. It’s just not, and it won’t happen."

When reached for comment, Hochul's office directed Fox News Digital to the governor's remarks to Spectrum News NY1 during a Q&A with the press in New York City on Wednesday.

"Well, that's certainly [voters'] prerogative to decide who they want to lead Israel," Hochul told NY1. "It's not mine. But I was simply asked a question, if you see how it's framed. Would your life be a lot easier if Netanyahu was not the leader of Israel? I'm like, yes."

FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER

Tuesday's vote marked a major test for Netanyahu's political future as Israelis headed to the polls for the first time since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre.

"I am proud of Israel's democratic process," Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon told Fox News Digital. "Yesterday, millions of Israelis exercised their democratic right to vote, with voter turnout reaching one of the highest levels recorded in Israel this century – 77.7%. The Israeli people have made their voices heard, and their democratic choice deserves to be respected."

"I encourage all elected officials in the United States to respect Israel's democratic process, just as Israel respects the democratic process in the United States," Danon added. "Our shared commitment to democracy is a fundamental pillar of the strong and enduring partnership between our two countries."

With about 70% of the votes tallied as of Wednesday morning, partial results reported by Israeli media showed Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc leading with 54 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, versus 47 for the main opposition and 19 for Arab parties.

item.title: DOJ fires back at Dem AG over Election Day guidance telling officials when to call cops on federal agents
item.description: The Justice Department slammed Jay Jones' Election Day guidance as "bluster" after Virginia advised poll workers to call police on DOJ monitors.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department blasted Virginia Democratic Attorney General Jay Jones' Election Day guidance as "bluster and political posturing," pushing back against his 10-page directive advising local election officials to call police when federal agents approach polling places and to document their activities.

The Oct. 15 bulletin, jointly issued by Jones' office and the Virginia Department of Elections, outlines how officials should respond to federal agents, scrutinize requests from DOJ election monitors and prepare for potential federal demands for ballots and voting equipment.

The dispute comes as conservative litigation firm America First Legal pursues records concerning the state's warnings about potential federal election interference, which Fox News Digital has learned.

"The Virginia Attorney General's performative actions attack a strawman," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "DOJ's election monitors will be engaging in the same routine monitoring we've done for decades."

SPANBERGER AG DRAWS FIRE OVER TWO-FRONT FIGHT AGAINST TRUMP ENFORCEMENT AGENDA

"We're hopeful local election officials in Virginia continue their longstanding practice of allowing DOJ election monitors into polling places to evaluate for compliance with federal law," the spokesperson continued. "The Virginia AG's statement reads as nothing more than bluster and political posturing for his own self-interested purposes."

DOJ has already announced it plans to send election monitors to Democratic-heavy Fairfax and Prince William Counties.

Del. Wren Williams, R-Stuart, an attorney who battled Jones over Democrats’ failed redistricting-related litigation, said Jones has his election-security priorities backward.

"Jay Jones wants poll workers collecting ICE agents’ badge numbers, but God forbid they verify a voter’s ID," Williams said. "Plus, I thought Democrats said illegals weren’t voting, so who exactly is Jones trying to protect?"

MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY

Virginia still requires voters to present identification or sign an identity confirmation statement, although legislation enacted this year eliminated Election Day challenges to individual voters' qualifications at polling places.

The blueprint noted that ELECT — the Virginia elections agency — received multiple inquiries about how to respond to federal representatives showing up at polls.

It instructed election officials to consult with lawyers and establish communications with local prosecutors and police:

"Having these discussions prior to Election Day ensures that election officials can provide their perspective to local law enforcement about what counts as intimidation and interference during elections, including issues related to the presence of unauthorized individuals."

"If, for example, an armed individual attempts to gain access to a polling location, officials should call local law enforcement immediately," it added in a section addressing unauthorized individuals and prohibited conduct.

The bulletin separately advises officials to consider contacting police and counsel if federal agents approach or enter polls, while cautioning against physically obstructing them.

Virginia State Sen. Danny Diggs, R-Poquoson — the former sheriff of York County — told Fox News Digital that in his 45 years in law enforcement he never saw an officer or official observer "make a polling place less safe."

"I routinely visited every polling place, inside and outside, while armed and in uniform and was always welcomed by election officials and voters. The Attorney General apparently thinks otherwise," Diggs said. He also called it "reckless" for the attorney general's game plan to urge election officials to confront federal observers.

On Page 4, the plan says ordinary DOJ monitors must obtain local authorization to enter polling locations, under rules similar to those for neutral observers.

If a DOJ monitor requests access, the plan prescribes that local registrars discuss the scope of the monitoring with the agency before consenting, and "consider asking whether DOJ is assessing compliance with civil or criminal federal laws."

The bulletin also advises election officials to consult attorneys and prepare to respond to federal subpoenas seeking ballots or voting equipment.

Fox News Digital reached out to Jones and ELECT for comment and a response to critics.

Jones, however, spoke out days earlier after launching a related new Voter Protection Section within his office.

"I was raised by people who understood that the right to vote was never simply given. Generations of Americans had to sacrifice, organize, and show extraordinary courage to claim that right," Jones said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital. "That history is personal to me, and it reminds us that the work of civil rights and voting rights is never finished.

"That is why we created a dedicated Voter Protection Section within the Office of the Attorney General. This work now has a permanent home, and a team focused every day on defending voting rights and enforcing Virginia law. Virginia votes every year, and protecting the franchise must be a year-round responsibility. In Virginia, the right to vote will be defended."

Virginia Beach attorney Tim Anderson also analyzed Jones' gameplan, calling it a "remarkable directive to election officials."

"While all this is happening, Virginia has eliminated the ability to challenge a voter's qualifications at the polling place," Anderson said.

"Think about what we're witnessing: The attorney general is preparing election officials to scrutinize federal law enforcement while Virginia has eliminated a longstanding Election Day safeguard for questioning voter eligibility," he said in a statement. "The bulletin identifies no specific planned unlawful federal operation in Virginia."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

America First Legal (AFL) exclusively told Fox News Digital on Tuesday it filed a public-records request Monday seeking legal analyses and communications behind the bulletin, records concerning Jones' newly launched Voter Protection Section and inquiries about federal election monitoring.

The dispute now turns on what evidence, if any, prompted Jones' office to prepare for potential federal interference at Virginia polling places, and whether the records sought by America First Legal will shed light on the attorney general's concerns ahead of Election Day.

item.title: Date-rape drug at center of Cornell sex assault allegations can leave victims unaware of surroundings
item.description: A former Cornell University student described feeling severe dissociation after taking ketamine before an alleged fraternity gang rape.
item.content:encoded:
An investigation into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity has thrust the illicit use of ketamine into the spotlight, calling attention to the powerful anesthetic’s use on college campuses as a date-rape drug.

The former Cornell student testified before the university’s hearing panel that ketamine made her feel "like her lights were on but no one was home," describing a state of "vague consciousness."

During an Oct. 23 appearance on "Fox & Friends," Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a Fox News contributor and addiction specialist in New York, warned that the drug’s physiological effects can leave people unable to defend themselves or understand their environment.

INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

"When you say the lights are on, but nobody’s home, that’s a pretty good way to describe it," Widmer said. "You can essentially have no awareness of your surroundings."

Ketamine affects NMDA receptors in the brain and can alter vital signs, according to the doctor.

"It can cause profound sedation, and it can cause dissociation, which is essentially the sensation of your brain not really being attached to your body," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While ketamine has legitimate medical uses — it was used as a battlefield anesthetic during the Vietnam War and remains FDA-approved for general anesthesia — the drug is also abused recreationally at parties, raves and nightclubs.

The Drug Enforcement Administration classifies ketamine as a Schedule III controlled substance and identifies it, alongside Rohypnol and GHB, as a drug that can be used to facilitate sexual assault. The agency says these substances can cause sedation, confusion and memory loss, leaving victims vulnerable.

When asked why ketamine falls into the category of date-rape drugs, Widmer said it can affect both cognitive function and physical awareness.

"There are a number of date-rape drugs that are out there, and ketamine does fall into that category because of what it can do to your sensorium," she added.

Widmer also warned about mixing ketamine with alcohol or other substances, which can compound the drugs’ effects and increase the risk of dangerous sedation and respiratory depression.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"They’re combining them with other substances, they’re combining them with alcohol, and that can compound the effects of these drugs," she said. "It can cause really profound sedation. It can be incredibly dangerous."

Widmer said her biggest concern is how parents discuss the dangers of drugs with their children, especially before sending them off to college.

"Everybody knows to say drugs are bad and not to do drugs, and you never know what you’re getting, but really understanding what some of these drugs can do is really important... that they’re not benign and that they can cause dissociation."

item.title: Federal judge who oversaw Maduro, Trump cases dead at 92
item.description: Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who denied Cilia Flores' bond request and oversaw the Nicolas Maduro torture case, died at age 92 of natural causes.
item.content:encoded:
Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who was overseeing the case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, died at the age of 92 on Tuesday.

Hellerstein had served as a U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York since 1998, after being appointed by then-President Bill Clinton. He had also presided over President Donald Trump's attempts to move his New York criminal case from state courts to federal courts.

The court said Hellerstein died of natural causes just short of his 93rd birthday.

TRUMP PICKS JAMES MCDONALD TO LEAD POWERFUL SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK AFTER JAY CLAYTON'S DEPARTURE

Hellerstein earned his J.D. and bachelor's degree from Columbia University, according to the Federal Judicial Center. He served in the U.S. Army, JAG Corps from 1957-1960 before 38 years of private practice prior to his judicial appointment.

DENVER MAN’S ESCAPE EXPOSES CHILLING TREN DE ARAGUA KIDNAPPING PLOT THAT LANDS TRIO IN PRISON

A new judge is set to be randomly assigned to handle the Maduro case following Hellerstein's passing.

Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are both charged with conspiracy to commit torture against Americans and others to stay in power, according to a superseding indictment filed in early October.

Maduro's government, according to the indictment, "presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens."

The torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims' families, including children," the indictment read.

MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM

The charge carries a maximum of life imprisonment if any of the alleged torture resulted in death, and a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison if not.

The indictment alleges Maduro and Flores "inflicted severe physical and mental pain and suffering to repress and punish political opposition, silence dissent and perceived dissent, preserve and protect the power and authority of the members of the conspiracy, and intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings."

MADURO'S ALLEGED 'BAG MAN' ALEX SAAB ARRESTED LESS THAN 3 YEARS AFTER BIDEN PARDON: REPORT

The pair, who face numerous other charges, were arrested in Venezuela in January during Operation Absolute Resolve. Maduro was originally charged with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices in a 2011 indictment that President Donald Trump's Department of Justice unsealed in 2020.

Flores was then charged in a superseding indictment in January with cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. They have pleaded not guilty, and a trial is scheduled for June 2027.

Flores appeared in court earlier this month for a bond hearing on her motion for release from jail. Her lawyers were requesting home confinement with GPS tracking, citing a heart condition and arguing she does not pose a danger to the community. Hellerstein denied the request.

Blackman described the issue as a longstanding grievance with all major media outlets and said he was quoted twice as a "conservative law professor" in New York Times articles in February.

"I just thought that was strange. So I went through the Westlaw archives and just sort of searched for 'liberal' law professors and 'conservative' law professors in the New York Times database, and it was far more likely that you’re identifying a conservative than a liberal. And those numbers are stacked because liberals are quoted even more often. So the numbers even have a greater disparity," he said during the conversation with Healy.

CONGRESS TO PUT AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION IN HOT SEAT OVER DEI RULES TIED TO LAW SCHOOL ACCREDITATION

"And this sort of reinforces, I think, a perception that both the academy and, frankly, the media views a liberal position as a neutral position. And the conservative position is the other, the outlier. And that’s why you have to have this sort of nomenclature, this sort of adjective to describe it," Blackman said.

He said he wrote a letter to the editor in February and the Times didn't publish it, but added that he appreciated Healy reaching out to him about it.

LEGACY MEDIA TRUST HITS NEW LOW WITH SWALWELL STORY LATEST EXAMPLE OF PROTECTING DEMS

Healy went on to acknowledge the validity of Blackman's critique: "I think there’s real truth to your critique and it’s something we need to do a better job on." 

"It can come off like The Times treats liberals as normal and conservatives as unique and worthy of labeling," Healy said. "In the legal academy, there are a lot of liberals, but that doesn’t justify it. I think we need to be more discerning about it."

NEW YORK TIMES PROBES NICHOLAS KRISTOF COLUMNS AFTER REPORT HE FAILED TO DISCLOSE CAMPAIGN DONOR CONNECTIONS

Fox News Digital reached out to the New York Times for comment.

Blackman argued that the label should reflect a professor's involvement in an issue rather than their political affiliation. He said, "And some of your reporters have said, well, 'Professor Blackman has filed briefs in support of the Trump administration', or 'has filed a brief in opposition to the Obama administration on health care,' or, you know, 'has filed a brief in support of the Texas attorney general' — whatever it happens to be. That's actually a data point that's useful because it shows a person has sort of a dog in the fight."

He said broad labels, such as conservative and liberal, don't tell the reader much.

"So it presumes that, well, because he’s conservative, you know, you should discount his views supporting Trump, or conversely, because the person’s liberal, you should perhaps discount their views supporting President Obama or President Biden, whoever it happens to be. I would — if you’re trying to build up trust and standards, I would focus on the potential reason for a conflict or bias, and not just how the person identifies politically," Blackman said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Curtis Houck, a managing editor at NewsBusters, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "It seems like Healy is aiming to go to Halloween parties this weekend as Captain Obvious. It's one thing to recognize you have a problem, but as most people are aware, that's only step one, and it can often be used to punt or not actually follow through on changes."

Houck added, "Healy, if pressed on camera, would probably try to back off or memory hole this conversation instead of making any concrete commitment to The Times doing any better. He's probably more upset that someone reached out to catch the paper red-handed instead of the fact that he — through his own journalism career — and his colleagues have spent more than a lifetime burying and/or smearing conservatives."

The Wall Street Journal's assistant editor to the editorial page, James Freeman, praised the NYT in a piece on Monday, and credited them for acknowledging a source's criticism.

item.title: El-Sayed accused Biden of exploiting 9/11 mastermind's killing in resurfaced attack: 'Troubling'
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed accused Joe Biden of exploiting the Ayman al-Zawahiri drone strike to bolster his party's approval before the midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
When American forces killed one of the architects of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed criticized then-President Joe Biden, accusing him of using the operation to boost his political standing rather than focusing on the significance of the strike.

On Aug. 1, 2022, Biden announced that Ayman al-Zawahiri had been killed in a U.S. drone strike.

"He was deeply involved in the planning of 9/11, one of the most responsible for the attacks that murdered 2,977 people on American soil," the president told the nation following the strike. Intelligence officials have long held that al-Zawahiri was involved in the planning behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks as well as other deadly assaults on Americans overseas.

CBS NEWS TAKES HEAT OVER REPORT ON DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED'S NOW-DELETED 9/11 POSTS

El-Sayed condemned al-Zawahiri as a terrorist in an essay, but criticized Biden for what he portrayed as an attempt to capitalize politically on the strike.

"President Biden is using the strike to bolster his approval here at home. It is troubling to watch yet another American president flog ‘War on Terror’ themes to resurrect a laggard term," El-Sayed wrote in 2022 for The New Republic. "This strike, then, offers the Biden administration a fig leaf, demonstrating that even in Taliban hands, Afghanistan is not off-limits for direct action against terrorist targets."

EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY

El-Sayed argued that Biden was using the killing of al-Zawahiri to bolster his political standing ahead of the looming midterm elections

He went on to argue that, if Biden was serious about "projecting strength in the Middle East," he would challenge some of the autocratic leaders in the region with whom the United States had traditionally aligned.

While El-Sayed criticized Biden's handling of the death of al-Zawahiri, he condemned the al-Qaeda leader in no uncertain terms, calling him a "craven terrorist" who "died with the blood of innocent civilians on his hands."

The Washington Free Beacon was the first to report on the newly unearthed essay.

ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS

El-Sayed has previously criticized other high-profile U.S. military and counterterrorism operations.

Similarly, when President Donald Trump ordered the 2020 drone strike of Iranian military leader Qassem Soleimani, El-Sayed warned that "one shouldn't kick a rabid dog." When President Barack Obama’s administration killed terrorist Anwar al-Awlaki, a U.S. citizen living in Yemen, El-Sayed characterized it as an "extrajudicial assassination."

El-Sayed has also compared Trump to Osama bin Laden, suggesting that both inspired people to engage in terrorism and that Trump should be held to account like bin Laden was. Bin Laden was killed by American operators in May 2011.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

item.title: GOP lawmakers urge Rubio to weigh visa restrictions on corrupt officials as Albania rocked by protests
item.description: Two Republican Congressmen urge Marco Rubio to impose visa restrictions on corrupt Albanian officials as violent protests demand Edi Rama's resignation.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Two Republican members of Congress sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressing concern over the state of NATO ally Albania’s democratic backsliding, urging the department to use its visa restriction authority against Albanian officials complicit in significant corruption.

"We write to express concern about the state of democracy and the rule of law in the Republic of Albania, a NATO ally and candidate for European Union membership. The United States has invested heavily in Albania's justice reforms and has a strong interest in their success. Recent events suggest that progress is fragile and, in key areas, at risk of reversal," the letter to Secretary Rubio said.

Specifically, the letter urges Secretary Rubio to use the State Department's authority under Section 7031(c) of the annual Department of State, Foreign Operations and Related Programs Appropriations Act to publicly designate Albanian officials and their immediate family members, if necessary, if credible information of involvement in significant corruption exists.

SERBIA’S LONGTIME LEADER FACES BIGGEST POLITICAL TEST AS STUDENTS MOUNT ELECTION CHALLENGE

The letter, written by Rep. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., and his Republican colleague, House Europe Subcommittee Chairman Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, requested the administration answer four key questions by Nov. 5.

In addition to asking the state department to commit to reviewing Albanian officials for designation under its visa restriction authority, the members of congress inquired about what assistance is being provided to Albania's broader justice reform efforts and whether the U.S. Embassy in Tirana is working with local officials to protect protesters and journalists.

The Republican representatives are also requesting an update on former Deputy Prime Minister Belinda Balluku, who was charged with interfering in public procurement for road construction. Prosecutors asked parliament in December 2025 to lift her immunity so she could be arrested, but Prime Minister Edi Rama called the request unconstitutional, and parliament has not allowed the arrest to proceed.

The members of congress say that Albania's anti-corruption institutions cannot succeed in rooting out corruption when political leaders shield the officials they investigate.

US LAWMAKERS SOUND ALARM AS VIOLENCE GRIPS NATO ALLY ALBANIA AMID ANTI-GOVERNMENT PROTESTS

Like fellow protesters in France and across Europe, tens of thousands have protested amid allegations of government corruption, inadequate education, unemployment and a lack of opportunity. The growing nationwide protest movement is driven by students and citizens also demanding accountability, an end to corruption and what they say is the restoration of democratic institutions and the rule of law.

Demonstrations broke out in the capital, Tirana, two weeks ago, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. The protests quickly turned violent as demonstrators lobbed Molotov cocktails at the Education Ministry and clashed with police.

Protesters also took aim at Rama’s Socialist Party headquarters in Tirana, squaring off with riot police who had been dispatched to protect government property.

Rama blamed "foreign hands who do not want Albania in the European Union and who promote the masks that claim to represent students, but who in fact, more than students, represent organized crime itself."

So far, the prime minister has refused to resign but has proposed entering into dialogue with the protesters.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

The violence taking place across Albania is a worrying sign for a country struggling to maintain its democracy and continue the path to EU accession.

"Congress is deeply concerned about the situation in Albania as the government uses excessive force against citizens who are demanding accountability and clean institutions. Corruption and narcotrafficking associated with the Rama government must be countered," Rep. Wilson told Fox News Digital in a statement.

The turmoil in Albania comes as the country has long sought European Union membership, which began in 2014 when it became an official candidate for accession. While the 2025 annual European Commission report stated that Albania made significant strides in judicial reforms and combating organized crime, the continued allegations of corruption in the Rama government and the current violence taking place will complicate its path to EU membership.

The student protests in Albania mirror the mass protests that took place in neighboring Serbia, where a student-led political movement toppled longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić.

"Vucic’s defeat by a student-backed movement, following nearly two years of demonstrations over corruption and government accountability, is a striking parallel with the unrest now confronting Rama in Albania, where protests have been ongoing for over 150 days," Agim Nesho, former Albanian ambassador to the U.N. and U.S., told Fox News.

"In Albania, students and other citizens have been demonstrating since May, with the latest wave of daily protests intensifying demands for the resignation of a prime minister who has governed for more than 13 years with rampant corruption and declining public services," Nesho added.

item.title: LEE ZELDIN: Biden's energy rules cost billions. Trump's EPA is lowering costs
item.description: The EPA proposal to overhaul Biden-era oil and gas rules is expected to save Americans $45 billion and unleash 210 million more barrels of oil.
item.content:encoded:
So much of America runs on oil and gas. It's fuel in vehicles and heat in homes. It's the diesel in the tractor that grows your food and the truck that hauls it to your grocery store. When it costs more to produce and supply goes down, you pay more for almost everything.

That's why President Donald Trump and I were in Lubbock, Texas, Tuesday to announce our biggest step yet to fix one of the Biden administration's costliest mistakes. EPA's new proposal to overhaul the Biden-era oil and natural gas rules is expected to save Americans $45 billion. It would also unleash an estimated 210 million more barrels of American oil and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.

In 2024, the Biden EPA slapped one-size-fits-all mandates on oil and gas producers, from the biggest companies to families with a single well. By its own estimate, the rule would cost $18 billion and push natural gas prices higher, and even those estimates were too low. Worse, the Biden EPA refused to admit what producers told us again and again: these rules would shut down existing wells and keep new ones from ever opening.

THE IRAN WAR DIDN'T MAKE YOUR HEATING BILL THIS HIGH. BLUE-STATE ENERGY POLICY DID

Producers don't absorb those costs. You do. You pay at the pump, on your heating bill and at the checkout line, because farmers paying more for diesel have to charge more for their crops.

Nobody was hit harder than America's marginal well owners. About 783,000 of the nation's oil and gas wells, roughly 79%, are small, low-producing wells, many on family land. Families use them to heat their homes, run their farm equipment and build their retirement. The Biden rule would have forced mass closures of these wells.

BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK

Our proposal fixes that. We are proposing separate, workable standards for different kinds of well sites, so a family's stripper well isn't treated like a major operation. We are proposing to end the so-called super emitter program, which is unnecessary, ineffective and built on shaky legal ground. And for the natural gas that comes up alongside oil, we are restoring a commonsense standard: 95% efficient flaring or other controls, instead of a mandate that every bit of it reach a sales line that simply doesn't exist in many producing areas.

Protecting human health and the environment is EPA's core mission, and that isn't changing. The Clean Air Act requires standards that sources can actually achieve. The Biden EPA touted "zero emissions" requirements while ignoring that existing rules already required 95% reductions, then stuffed its rule with exemptions to paper over the gap.

TRUMP'S EPA REFORMS ARE A HUGE BOOST TO MANUFACTURERS, BUT THERE'S MORE RED TAPE TO CUT: EXPERT

We are writing rules that match reality, and we want to hear from the states and operators who know it best.

Beyond Tuesday’s announcement, the Trump EPA has racked up a series of wins that have proven popular everywhere the president has traveled, and Texas is no exception. Over the past year, the agency finalized a record $1.6 trillion in deregulatory savings, a historic effort that is advancing consumer choice and lowering costs on vehicles, energy, food, and more with commonsense actions that prove we can protect the environment and grow the economy at the same time.

The repeal of the 2009 Obama-era Endangerment Finding alone delivered $1.3 trillion in cost savings and made vehicles more affordable, while eliminating the federal incentive behind the almost universally hated start/stop feature that killed engines at every red light. That stands in stark contrast to the $1.3 trillion in unnecessary rules the Biden EPA piled onto American families and the economy.

The Trump EPA has also moved aggressively to reverse the Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) deratements that left farmers and truckers stranded on the side of the road and in the field. John Deere has now updated all major models for the fall 2026 harvest to align with EPA’s guidance, and the agency is finalizing a new deregulatory proposal to permanently remove all DEF deratement requirements on new vehicles, non-road equipment and engines. Building on that work, EPA has protected Americans’ Right to Repair their own tractors and non-road equipment under the Clean Air Act, and this past July took further action to advance the Freedom to Fix in accordance with President Trump’s memo.

The math here is simple. When American producers can produce, America wins through lower gas and diesel prices, lower heating bills, lower grocery costs and more good-paying energy jobs. Lower costs at the well and higher energy supplies mean more money in your wallet.

President Trump promised to end the war on American energy and this proposal is one more promise kept.

item.title: Dolores Huerta, United Farm Workers co-founder who accused César Chavez of sex abuse, dead at 96
item.description: The longtime labor organizer and civil rights activist helped build a national movement advocating for agricultural workers after beginning her career as a schoolteacher.
item.content:encoded:
Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor activist who co-founded the United Farm Workers union and spent decades fighting for better working conditions for America's agricultural workers, has died. She was 96.

Huerta died at her home on Wednesday in Bakersfield, California, surrounded by her close family, her foundation announced.

Svante Myrick, president of the progressive advocacy group People For the American Way, where Huerta served on the board of directors for 22 years, remembered her as "unstoppable," in a statement remembering her legacy.

"Dolores Huerta was one of the fiercest and most consequential activists in our nation’s history," Myrick said. "She was the first to get started in the morning and the last to quit at the end of the day."

Born in New Mexico and raised by a single mother in California's San Joaquin Valley, Huerta began her career as a schoolteacher before helping establish a local chapter of a grassroots organization that challenged segregation and police brutality.

CALIFORNIA DEMOCRATS DISTANCE THEMSELVES FROM FAMED PRO-UNION ACTIVIST AFTER BOMBSHELL REPORT

Eventually, her focus turned to labor organizing, and together with César Chavez, whom she'd later accuse of sexual abuse, she built the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. Four years later, that association merged with another organization to form the United Farm Workers union.

Six decades after its founding, the United Farm Workers remains the nation's longest-standing labor union representing agricultural workers.

Huerta herself was one of the most enduring and influential labor leaders in the country, becoming known for her rallying cry, "Sí, se puede!" 

In English, the slogan translates to "Yes, it can be done," reflecting her sincere belief that ordinary people can affect political change.

Beyond her work to improve the lives of those working in America's fruit and vegetable fields, many of whom are immigrants, Huerta became a prominent civil rights and women's rights advocate, combating discrimination and fighting for gender equality in a labor movement that was dominated by men at the time.

DOLORES HUERTA RECEIVES NATIONAL PRIZE FOR PUBLIC SERVICE

Huerta was one of the leaders behind the Delano grape strike, which lasted from September 1965 to July 1970. She, along with a coalition of Mexican and Filipino farmhands, accused grape growers in Delano, California, of exploiting their workers by underpaying them.

Thousands of farmworkers walked off California's grape fields in 1965, sparking a labor movement that gained momentum in the years that followed. Huerta played a pivotal role in expanding the strike into a nationwide consumer boycott of grapes.

In the summer of 1970, the strike ended after the United Farm Workers union signed off on collective bargaining agreements that covered 10,000 workers.

Huerta received numerous awards throughout her career, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. Presenting her with the award in 2012, then-President Barack Obama praised her decades of activism and joked that he had borrowed her famous slogan, "Sí, se puede," for his 2008 presidential campaign.

DEMS FACE RECKONING AFTER PUTTING DECEASED LABOR LEADER ON PEDESTAL AS SEXUAL ABUSE ALLEGATIONS EMERGE

Earlier this year, Huerta publicly accused César Chavez of raping her in 1966 after driving her out to a grape field in Delano, where the strike was unfolding.

Huerta's account was published in The New York Times in March alongside two other women who say Chavez sexually abused them as girls during the 1970s.

Huerta also told The Times there was another incident between her and Chavez in August 1960, when he allegedly pressured her into having sex with him in a hotel room while on a work trip in San Juan Capistrano in Southern California.

Huerta said she became pregnant following both encounters with Chavez, who died in 1993, and later arranged for the children to be adopted and raised by other families, according to a statement she released addressing the allegations.

She said she kept both the alleged assaults and the children secret for decades out of fear that others in the Latino civil rights movement would not believe her. She also worried that speaking out against Chavez, one of the movement's most prominent figures, would ultimately damage the cause and their shared objectives.

Despite her revelation, Huerta encouraged people to continue fighting for their rights and said the labor movement was bigger than her or Chavez.

Huerta's lifelong partner starting in the early 1970s was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, whom she had four kids with. She also had seven children from two previous marriages.

Even into her 90s, Huerta remained politically active, delivering speeches, attending rallies and speaking out on issues ranging from civil rights to national politics.
